pedagogy.summary: Having named and ordered the eight planets, children now give each a memorable identity: Mercury the smallest and closest; Venus the hottest; Mars the red planet (rusty iron in its soil); Jupiter the largest, with its Great Red Spot storm; Saturn with its spectacular rings; Uranus tipped over on its side; Neptune the farthest and bitterly cold. At 7–9 the aim is a vivid, sticky signature fact per planet plus a little comparison ('Jupiter is far bigger than Earth', 'Venus is hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is closer'), building curiosity and a sense that each world is genuinely different. The one 'why' worth teaching is Mars's colour — iron oxide (rust) in its rocks — because it links a striking observation to a cause children can grasp. Best practice uses real images (these are among the most captivating pictures in science), memorable hooks/comparisons, and a card-sorting/matching approach so features attach to the right planet. Keep facts accurate but light; this is identity-building, not planetary geology, and one counter-intuitive comparison (hottest is Venus, not closest Mercury) is worth surfacing to spark thinking.
bestPractices: Give each planet ONE vivid signature fact and hook it to a strong real image (the Great Red Spot, Saturn's rings, red Mars) so the feature is memorable and image-anchored
Use surprising comparisons to provoke thinking: Venus is hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun (its thick atmosphere traps heat) — an early cause-and-effect worth flagging
Teach the one causal 'why' explicitly: Mars looks red because its rocks/soil contain iron oxide — rust — the same stuff that makes old iron go orange
Practise with matching/sorting (feature ↔ planet cards) so distinctive features attach to the correct planet rather than blurring together
Keep numbers/scale light and comparative ('much bigger', 'far colder') rather than exact, leaving quantitative scale to the dedicated later topic
keyRepresentations: A gallery of real planet images, each captioned with its signature feature (the naming/identity reference)
Feature ↔ planet matching cards (rings → Saturn, Great Red Spot → Jupiter, red/rust → Mars…)
A simple comparison line-up (relative size; hottest → coldest) to support 'bigger/hotter/colder than' talk
A close-up of rusty Mars soil linked to everyday rust, explaining the red colour
commonMisconceptions: The closest planet to the Sun (Mercury) must be the hottest (Venus is hottest — its thick atmosphere traps heat)
Only Saturn has rings (all four gas giants have ring systems; Saturn's are just the brightest and most obvious)
Mars is red because it is hot / on fire (it is cold; the red is iron oxide — rust — in its rocks)
The Great Red Spot is a feature on the surface (Jupiter has no solid surface; the Spot is a giant long-lived storm in its atmosphere)
All planets are roughly Earth-like / you could stand on any of them (the gas giants have no solid surface; conditions range from scorching to freezing)

learn.summary: Help children aged 7–9 give each of the eight planets a vivid, memorable signature identity anchored to real photographs: Mercury smallest/closest, Venus hottest, Mars red (rust), Jupiter largest with the Great Red Spot, Saturn with bright rings, Uranus tipped on its side, Neptune farthest and bitterly cold. The aim is identity-building with light comparison ('Jupiter is far bigger than Earth'), one causal 'why' worth teaching (Mars's red = iron oxide/rust), and one counter-intuitive comparison worth surfacing (Venus, not closest Mercury, is hottest, because its thick atmosphere traps heat).

activities.title: Visit Eight Very Different Worlds
feedback: If a child says Mars is red because it is hot or on fire: Mars is actually a cold desert planet; its red comes from rust (iron oxide) in the soil, which has nothing to do with heat.
If a child expects Mercury to be hottest because it is closest: Venus is hotter — its thick atmosphere traps heat like a blanket, while airless Mercury lets its heat leak away, especially at night.
If a child thinks the Great Red Spot is a mark on the ground: Jupiter has no solid surface to mark; the Spot is a giant, long-lasting storm in Jupiter's gases, wider than the whole Earth.
Reinforce correct matches by naming the feature with the planet aloud, so the feature attaches to the right world.
activities.rationale: Per-planet attribute learning is well suited to real imagery captioned with one sticky fact; a tap-to-reveal gallery (optional, untested interaction example) lets stunning photographs carry the wonder, and predict-then-reveal flaps surface the two surprises (Mars's rust; Venus hottest) as moments of designed insight rather than facts to memorise.
sourceClaims: Each planet has distinctive features taught at primary level — Mercury smallest/closest, Venus hottest (thick CO2 atmosphere traps heat), Mars red from iron oxide, Jupiter largest with the Great Red Spot storm, Saturn's prominent rings, Uranus's extreme axial tilt, Neptune farthest and cold.
Mars appears red because its surface rocks and dust are rich in iron oxide (rust).
learnerActions: Look at a real photograph of each planet alongside one bold signature fact: Saturn's bright rings, Jupiter's swirling Great Red Spot, Uranus lying on its side, tiny Mercury hugging the Sun, rusty-red Mars, bitterly cold Neptune farthest out.

For Mars, first say what you think 'red' might mean, then reveal: a close-up of rusty soil beside an old rusty nail — 'Mars is red for the same reason old iron goes orange: rust (iron oxide) in its rocks.'
For the 'which planet is hottest?' question, make a prediction before revealing the answer: it is Venus, not Mercury, because Venus is wrapped in a thick blanket of air that traps the Sun's heat.
Link each planet back to its place in the order of the eight planets.
activities.intendedInsight: Each planet is a genuinely distinct world with its own striking feature; and a planet's temperature depends on more than its distance from the Sun — its atmosphere matters too.

activities.title: Match the Feature to the Right Planet
feedback: If a child believes rings belong to Saturn alone as the only ringed planet: Saturn's rings are the brightest and most obvious, but all four giant outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) have ring systems.
If the hottest-planet answer is Mercury: distance from the Sun is not the only factor — Venus's thick atmosphere traps heat, making it hotter than closer Mercury.
Confirm a correct 'why is Mars red' choice by restating that the red is rust (iron oxide) in the rocks, not heat.
activities.rationale: Matching and selection give a crisp consolidation check that each signature feature has landed on the right planet. Note this is recognition-style work: it checks that facts attach correctly but does not by itself elicit independent explanation of the causal ideas.
sourceClaims: Each planet has distinctive features taught at primary level — Mercury smallest/closest, Venus hottest (thick CO2 atmosphere traps heat), Mars red from iron oxide, Jupiter largest with the Great Red Spot storm, Saturn's prominent rings, Uranus's extreme axial tilt, Neptune farthest and cold.
Mars appears red because its surface rocks and dust are rich in iron oxide (rust).
learnerActions: Match each feature to its planet: rings → Saturn, Great Red Spot → Jupiter, red/rust → Mars, tilted on its side → Uranus, smallest and closest → Mercury, hottest → Venus, farthest and very cold → Neptune.
Answer: 'Which planet is the hottest?' — choosing from options that include the tempting Mercury (closest) distractor.
Answer: 'Why is Mars red?' — choosing rust/iron oxide rather than heat or fire.
State one distinctive feature for at least six of the eight planets in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: Distinctive features stay attached to the correct planet rather than blurring into a single list of names.

activities.title: Order and Build the Fact Files
feedback: If a child orders by distance when ordering by temperature: remind them Venus's trapped heat breaks the simple 'closer = hotter' pattern.
Encourage comparative language ('much bigger', 'far colder') rather than exact numbers, which belong to a later scale topic.
activities.rationale: An active sorting/build task adds engagement and practises comparison talk. The core objective remains attribute recall, so ordering supports but does not replace the gallery and matching work; keep scale light and comparative at this age.
sourceClaims: Each planet has distinctive features taught at primary level — Mercury smallest/closest, Venus hottest (thick CO2 atmosphere traps heat), Mars red from iron oxide, Jupiter largest with the Great Red Spot storm, Saturn's prominent rings, Uranus's extreme axial tilt, Neptune farthest and cold.
learnerActions: Drag or place the planets into order from hottest to coldest by typical (average) temperature, accepting Uranus and Neptune in either order as the two coldest, then from smallest to largest, and talk through the ordering using 'bigger/hotter/colder than'.
Assemble each planet's fact card from feature tiles (image + signature feature + one comparison).
Say at least one comparison aloud, e.g. 'Jupiter is much bigger than Earth' or 'Venus is hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is closer.'
activities.intendedInsight: Planets can be compared along size and temperature, and ordering them makes the surprising cases (Venus hotter than closer Mercury) stand out.

activities.title: Explain the Puzzle: Why Is Venus Hotter?
feedback: Full understanding: the child explains Venus is hottest because its thick atmosphere traps heat while Mercury's escapes, names features for several planets, and attributes Mars's red to rust rather than heat.
Partial: the child accepts Venus is hottest and names features but cannot say WHY an atmosphere makes the difference — introduce the atmosphere-as-blanket idea explicitly.
Gap: the child insists Mercury must be hottest (running distance as the only factor) or ties Mars's colour to heat — reteach the trapping-heat idea and separate colour (rust) from temperature.
activities.rationale: A short constructed explanation lets the child voice the causal 'why', which selection tasks cannot fully reveal. Asking the child to explain surfaces whether they hold the distance-only rule or the richer atmosphere idea.
sourceClaims: Each planet has distinctive features taught at primary level — Mercury smallest/closest, Venus hottest (thick CO2 atmosphere traps heat), Mars red from iron oxide, Jupiter largest with the Great Red Spot storm, Saturn's prominent rings, Uranus's extreme axial tilt, Neptune farthest and cold.
learnerActions: Respond to the prompt: 'Mercury is closest to the Sun, so you might expect it to be hottest. But Venus is hotter than Mercury. How can a planet that is further from the Sun end up hotter? Tell me WHY.'

Explain in your own words that Venus's thick atmosphere of gases traps the Sun's heat like a blanket and lets it escape only very slowly, while Mercury has almost no atmosphere so its heat leaks away.

Consider follow-up questions: What does a thick atmosphere do to the heat a planet gets? Which matters more for how hot a planet is — only distance, or atmosphere too? If Mars is red because of rust, does that tell us it is hot, or something else? Why can't Jupiter's Great Red Spot be a mark painted on the ground?
activities.intendedInsight: A planet's temperature is shaped by its atmosphere as well as its distance from the Sun; the 'closer = hotter' rule alone cannot explain Venus.

constraints: Keep facts accurate but light: this is identity-building, not planetary geology; aim for one sticky signature fact per planet plus simple comparisons.
Keep numbers and scale comparative ('much bigger', 'far colder') rather than exact; leave quantitative scale to a dedicated later topic.

Matching and multiple-choice tasks are recognition checks: they confirm features are attached to the right planet but do not elicit independent explanation of causal ideas (use the explanation task for that).
Use real photographs where possible — these are among the most captivating images in science and anchor each feature in a concrete observation.

Correct common errors explicitly: all four giant outer planets have rings (Saturn's are just brightest); Mars is cold, its red is rust not heat; the Great Red Spot is a storm in gas, not a surface mark; the giant outer planets have no solid surface to stand on.

A fly-through or 3D model can be engaging but is not required here; spatial scale belongs to the later scale topic rather than this attribute-recall topic. Open dialogue can also teach and is not inferior per se — it is simply not the focus for securing per-planet recall at this age.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (planet overviews and 'why is Mars red') are marked verified:false in the source row; only the DfE National Curriculum citation is marked verified. Treat the specific factual claims as plausible but not independently re-checked here.

The DfE Year 5 'Earth and space' citation supports the topic's curriculum placement at primary level; it is retained here as context rather than as per-activity sourceClaim support for any specific teaching method.

The source states Venus's heat trapping as a 'runaway greenhouse effect' in the assessment answer; for age 7–9 this has been kept at the 'thick atmosphere traps heat like a blanket' level, which is accurate and age-appropriate.

Predict-then-reveal flaps and tap-to-reveal galleries are described as optional interaction examples that make the learning mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory mechanisms and their efficacy is not established by the sources.

'Gas giants' is used informally in the original for all four outer planets; Uranus and Neptune are often classified as ice giants. Both learner-facing feedback and the developer constraints now say 'giant outer planets' for precision while keeping the primary-level simplicity.

probeDeeper: What does a thick atmosphere do to the heat a planet gets from the Sun?
If Mars is red because of rust, does that tell us it's hot — or something else?
Why can't Jupiter's Great Red Spot be a mark painted on the ground?
Which matters more for how hot a planet is: only its distance from the Sun, or its atmosphere too?
assess.correctAnswer: Venus is the hottest planet even though Mercury is closer to the Sun because Venus is wrapped in a very thick atmosphere of gases that traps the Sun's heat like a blanket and won't let it escape (a runaway greenhouse effect). Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so its heat leaks away, especially at night. So distance from the Sun isn't the only thing that sets a planet's temperature — its atmosphere matters too. (Mars, by the way, looks red because its rocks and dust are full of iron oxide — rust.)

errorPatterns.pattern: the planet closest to the Sun must be the hottest ('Mercury has to be hottest because it's nearest')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce the atmosphere-as-blanket idea: Venus's thick gases trap heat while airless Mercury lets it escape; temperature depends on more than distance.
errorPatterns.distractor: Mercury must really be the hottest planet, because it's the closest one to the Sun.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child insists Mercury must be hottest, or refuses to believe Venus is hotter, running distance as the only factor

errorPatterns.pattern: Mars is red because it is extremely hot, on fire, or made of lava
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain the red is rust — iron oxide in the soil and dust; Mars is actually a cold desert planet, colour has nothing to do with temperature.
errorPatterns.distractor: Mars is red because it is extremely hot, like fire.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child links Mars's red colour to heat or fire

errorPatterns.pattern: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a solid painted mark or a hole ('a red patch on the surface')
errorPatterns.nextMove: The Great Red Spot is a giant, long-lasting STORM in Jupiter's gases, wider than the whole Earth; Jupiter has no solid surface to mark.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child treats the Great Red Spot as a fixed surface marking on a solid planet

responseLevels.gap: Runs 'closest = hottest' and denies or cannot explain Venus; ties Mars's colour to heat.
responseLevels.full: Explains Venus is hottest because its thick atmosphere traps heat while Mercury's is lost, states distinctive features for several planets, and correctly attributes Mars's red to rust rather than heat.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts Venus is hottest and names some planet features, but cannot say WHY an atmosphere makes the difference, or gives features without the comparison.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun, so you might expect it to be the hottest. But actually Venus is hotter than Mercury. How can a planet that is FURTHER from the Sun end up hotter? Tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child running the simple rule 'closer to the Sun = hotter' cannot explain how Venus beats Mercury and may deny it. A child who knows an atmosphere can trap heat resolves the puzzle. The 'why' tier separates the distance-only rule from the idea that a planet's atmosphere shapes its temperature.
